newsitem.title: USA: Dow index ends strong after a week of record highs.
newsitem.headline: Dow index ends strong after a week of record highs.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average ended on a strong note Friday, setting its fourth record in a week as solid corporate earnings reports stoked buying on the eve of Black Monday's ninth anniversary.

The Dow closed up 35.03 points at a new high of 6,094.23, surpassing Thursday's record of 6,059.20. It was the Dow's 31st closing high for 1996, coming just days after it closed above the 6,000 mark for the first time on Monday.
For the week, the Dow gained 124.85 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,319 to 1,046 on heavy volume of 467 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Among other indices, the Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 3.83 points to 710.82, its fourth record this week. The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 1.91 to 378.32, a new high.

"We have slow economic growth, inflation is not a problem and by and large, companies are hitting or beating earnings estimates," said William LeFevre, a senior market analyst at Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum.
The index of 30-blue-chip stocks would have racked up an even bigger gain, without the downward pressure exerted by Philip Morris -- a key component.
The company's stock sank 5-1/8 to 92-1/4 as tobacco shares were hammered by news that scientists claimed they had established the first direct link on a cellular level between smoking and cancer.
Weaker tobacco shares included Loews Corp., off 1-5/8 to 80, RJR Nabisco Holdings, off 3/4 to 26-3/4, and smokeless tobacco maker UST Inc., off 5/8 to 29-1/8.
But the stock market managed to sidestep the drops in Philip Morris and Xerox, which was down 8-1/8 to 48-7/8 after reporting disappointing third-quarter results.

"We're still in a bull market cycle that started several years ago," "said Merrill Lynch chief technical analyst Richard McCabe. "We may have periodic hesitations but it's not the final top yet. We may go up another 100-200 Dow points by year end."
But he cautioned that he saw a few signs "that we're in the seventh or eighth inning of the game."
Saturday marks the ninth anniversary of Black Monday, or Oct. 19, 1987, when the Dow plummeted 508.00 points or 22.61 percent.
"Here we are nine years after the event and all sorts of people remember it well," LeFevre said.

"But we're up almost 250 percent from the crash or 4,320 points. So yes, there may be some October jitters but hey, if 1,000 points were chopped off it's still a good run," he said. "The October jitters are probably for the bears to justify their stance."

Helping to boost the Dow index was International Business Machines, which jumped 3-7/8 to 129-3/8 prior to the release Monday of its third-quarter earnings. Some traders were hopeful of an upside surprise.
Among other shares, Iomega rose 1-3/16 to 24-1/16 after the desk-drive maker reported earnings late Thursday that were better than Wall Street expected.
Microsoft lost 3/4 to 134-3/4. SoundView Financial downgraded the software maker.
Vantive Corp. shed 9-1/2 to 31-1/4 after warning that its revenue growth will be flat for the next two quarters, analysts said. Vantive officials were not available for comment.

McDonald's lost 1/2 to 46. The fast food giant posted quarterly results that just missed Wall Street's target. The company also reported that its operating performance was not keeping pace with its goals and third-quarter operating income fell from last year.
The Nasdaq Composite index was up 0.52 of a point at 1,242.48. The American Stock Exchange index rose 1.64 to 579.03.
The average NYSE share was up 20 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was at a new high of 6,943.797 up 28.264 or 0.41 percent.
